source_read: Publisher HTML (APA PsycNet, open access, Psychology of Addictive Behaviors 2023;37(6):723-733), read in full in my own browser tab via https://doi.org/10.1037/adb0000919: abstract, introduction, Method, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, footnotes, author note (funding, conflicts, registration). The vignette and Table 1 are images: screenshots of my tab showed them blank when the article was scrolled, so each image's own URL was opened in the same tab and screenshotted (Table 1 enlarged with a CSS transform and read in two slices; all values legible). Online supplements (Files S1-S3, Table S1) not read.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of note; if anything one understatement. (1) 'Did not reliably change a pretend money task' and 'neither ... reliably changed what they gave or took': with the drug-use description, readers took more money (punishment 62.05 vs 53.96 pence, Welch t(1557.96) = 2.81, p = .005, significant at the study's alpha of .01; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), which the study's rule calls inconclusive only because the interval also reaches below its 0.20 bound; the paper's own Discussion makes the same simplification. Better: 'a small difference in money taken that the study could not show to be more than trivial'. (2) 'Large differences by the usual standard' fits d 0.87 and 0.95; 0.78 is just under Cohen's 0.8. (3) 'No personal or close-family history of substance use or psychiatric diagnoses' can be read as excluding anyone who had used drugs; the self-confirmed exclusion was of a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis in oneself or a known close relative. (4) 'A university participation scheme': the paper says research participation schemes (SONA), plural, across several institutions. (5) For the treatment framing, 'only inconclusive differences' is true of every self-report measure and of reward, but money taken (punishment) was equivalent (d -0.02), as the magnitude correctly says; the 'likely to succeed' version also said Alex was in a treatment programme rather than visiting a doctor.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude checks against the text and Table 1. Means: public stigma 50.59 vs 42.15 (RQ1), 49.62 vs 51.20 (RQ2); blame 8.61 vs 7.22 (RQ2); reward 248.11 vs 249.72 pence (RQ1). Directions on the means: drug use had lower social-distance scores (18.84 vs 23.76; lower = more distance), higher danger (17.37 vs 13.32) and lower blame (7.88 vs 8.81); the brain-disease label had higher social-distance scores (19.46 vs 18.38, i.e. less distance) and lower public stigma (49.62 vs 51.20), as the claim says; the uncertain (low-stability) framing had higher public stigma (52.15 vs 49.48), as the magnitude says. Recomputed from Table 1 means, SDs and ns: all 24 printed 'CI' intervals have the half-width of 98% intervals (z 2.326), none of 99% (z 2.576), e.g. social distance RQ1 98% 0.75-0.99 vs 99% 0.73-1.01, printed 0.74-0.99; this fits a TOST (1 - 2 alpha) interval labelled as 99%. Sample flow checks: 1,622 - 9 = 1,613; RQ1 1,613 - 53 = 1,560 = 819 + 741 (53 = 3.29%); RQ2 392 + 423 + 32 = 847 (3.78%); RQ3 362 + 383 + 102 = 847, so 102 is 12.04%, not the printed 11.96%. The vignette names no drug ('increasing drug use'), but the drug-use versions of four questionnaire items named opioid addiction (removed for the health-concern version), as the claim says.

anchors.extracted: Registered report: Stage 1 protocol given in-principle acceptance on 25 January 2022 via Peer Community In Registered Reports; materials, code and raw data on OSF; all manipulations, measures and exclusions reported.

2 (health condition: drug use vs health concern) x 2 (label: chronically relapsing brain disease vs problem) x 2 (treatment stability: low vs high) between-participants design. Eligibility self-confirmed: aged 18 or over, and neither having nor knowing a close relative with a previous or current substance use or psychiatric diagnosis. Recruited through research participation schemes (SONA), Prolific and social media; paid course credit or 5.00 pounds per hour. No country of residence stated.

1,622 recruited, 9 excluded (6 failed attention checks, 2 withdrew data, 1 implausible response time): 1,613 analysed; 36.5% aged 18-25 (called 'the majority'), 55.9% female, 77.1% White; details only in a supplement. Detectable equivalence ranges given the smallest cells: +/-0.21 for RQ1 (n = 741), +/-0.28 for RQ2 (n = 392), +/-0.30 for RQ3 (n = 362).

Alex is having serious trouble at home and work because of increasing drug use / a health concern; is now in a treatment program / has visited a doctor; staff say it is best understood as a chronically relapsing brain disease / a problem affecting many areas of life; high stability: Alex is committed to doing all they can to ensure success after treatment; low stability: the doctor says it may be long-term and could worsen, but could improve if treatment starts now. No drug is named.

anchors.locator: Method › Measures › Stigma and Attribution Assessment, 1st paragraph; Personal and Perceived Public Stigma Measure, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Stigma and Attribution Assessment: 22 items, five subscales (social distance, perceived danger, prognostic optimism, blame attribution, e.g. the opioid addiction being genetic in origin, and need for continued care), 1-6 agreement, summed; four items adapted for the health-concern version by removing the term opioid addiction; lower scores = more social distance, lower blame, lower optimism; only four alphas printed for five subscales (.88, .79, .70, .69). Public stigma measure: 23 items, four subscales, 1-4, summed into one score, higher = more stigma (alphas .70-.91).

anchors.locator: Method › Measures › Financial Discrimination Task, 1st paragraph; Method › Analytic Strategy, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Sham 'Psy-Learn' platform: participants watch the vignette person's six cognitive trials (always 50% correct) and give a reward of 0-100 pence for each correct answer and a punishment of 0-100 pence for each incorrect one (each summed over 3 trials, 0-300). Analysis: Welch t tests plus TOST equivalence tests (TOSTER), bounds d -0.20 to 0.20, alpha .01; effect called meaningful if different from zero and the stated 99% CI lies outside the bounds, equivalent if not different and inside, inconclusive if the interval overlaps both.

anchors.locator: Results › Research Question 1 (1st paragraph of Results); Table 1, RQ1 columns
anchors.extracted: 53 (3.29%) failed the manipulation check; drug use n = 819 vs health concern n = 741. Prognostic optimism -0.06 (-0.18 to 0.06) and reward -0.03 (-0.14 to 0.09): equivalent. Continued care 0.09 (-0.03 to 0.21) and punishment 0.14 (0.02-0.26): inconclusive. Table 1 means (SD), drug use vs concern: social distance 18.84 (5.46) vs 23.76 (5.87); danger 17.37 vs 13.32; blame 7.88 vs 8.81; public stigma 50.59 (8.86) vs 42.15 (8.99), t(1537.61) = 18.65; reward 248.11 vs 249.72 pence; punishment 62.05 vs 53.96 pence, t(1557.96) = 2.81, p = .005.

Social distance -0.23, danger 0.19, blame -0.11, optimism -0.17, continued care 0.11, public stigma 0.31 (0.14-0.48), reward -0.13: all inconclusive; punishment -0.02 (-0.19 to 0.16): equivalent. anchors.locator: Results (all three paragraphs) and Table 1: editors' recomputation
anchors.extracted: From the Table 1 means, SDs and ns, every printed interval (24 of 24) has the width of a 98% interval, not a 99% one: e.g. RQ1 public stigma 98% 0.83-1.07, 99% 0.81-1.09, printed 0.82-1.07; RQ2 blame 98% 0.37-0.71, 99% 0.36-0.72, printed 0.38-0.71.

The blame subscale's three items attribute the problem to a disease process (e.g. genetic origin), so a higher 'blame' score with the brain-disease label means more attribution to brain pathology, not more personal blame; the authors contrast this with Kelly et al. (2021), whose results ran the other way on most subscales.

On the money task, health condition was inconclusive for punishment and equivalent for reward, and label and treatment framing were equivalent for punishment and inconclusive for reward; the authors read this as self-reported stigma not appearing to translate reliably into overt discriminatory behaviour, while citing other studies (including Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010) that linked labels to a perceived need for punishment.

key_findings.note: Minor wording: the paper says research participation schemes (SONA), plural, across several institutions, not 'a university participation scheme'; sample.recruitment already has the plural. The claim copies the singular.
Directions re-checked on Table 1 means; all values match.

Accurate as worded. Worth adding that the punishment difference was significant at the study's alpha: Welch t(1557.96) = 2.81, p = .005, interval .02-.26 excluding zero; it is inconclusive only because the interval also overlaps the 0.20 bound.

'Likely to succeed' is the paper's own gloss of the high-stability text (Alex committed to doing all they can to ensure success after treatment); that version also places Alex in a treatment programme rather than visiting a doctor.

reporting_issues.note: Re-found blind and extended: all 24 printed intervals have the half-width of 98% intervals (z 2.326), none of 99%; RQ2 public stigma at 99% is -0.36 to 0.00, touching zero.
Checked: t = -2.55 with about 807 df gives two-sided p of about .011.
Re-found blind. Add RQ3 punishment: t printed 0.21 although the low-stability mean is lower (62.21 vs 63.16), so it should be -0.21.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 some concerns overall: per-protocol exclusions on manipulation checks and questionnaire wording that differs between the RQ1 arms; randomization, missing data and reporting low.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. One nuance: results_show says 'no reliable effect of any factor on rewards or punishments', echoing the authors' Discussion (5th paragraph), but the drug-use description went with more money taken (62.05 vs 53.96 pence, p = .005, d .14, interval .02-.26), a small difference that could not be shown to be trivial or meaningful.

missed: The paper calls the 36.5% aged 18-25 'the majority'; it is the largest group, not a majority (the card already says 'largest age band').

The paper says all Stigma and Attribution Assessment subscales had acceptable reliability (alpha > .70) in this sample, but one printed alpha is .69 (besides the card's point that only four alphas are printed for five subscales).

can_establish and the claim say 'without personal or family experience of substance use or psychiatric diagnoses', which can be read as excluding anyone who had used drugs; the self-confirmed exclusion was of a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis in oneself or a known close relative.
